content.thinking:
I'm noting a timing discrepancy: the flag toggle event is logged at 09:29:47, but the actual onset of errors (zero-division failures and flag-on evaluations) starts around 09:24, meaning the recorded flag switch happens well after the problem actually began — which undermines a candidate explanation that relies on that toggle as the cause.

I also can't verify the claimed human rollback at 09:31:25 since there's no confirming change event in the record, only a Slack claim, so it has to stay flagged as an unconfirmed assumption even though recovery timing does roughly line up with it.

Tracing the causal chain: account page requests started failing (error spike from baseline to peak, per G5309), caused by a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 that triggered once the monthly-spend-feature flag went on and routed traffic into that code path (per G971b/Gce95, with on-evaluations jumping to 40 of 200 at onset). The flag-on event itself is attributed to P1's admin switch, though its timestamp trails the actual onset, so I can't fully pin the mechanism — and I still don't know why the denominator hit zero, since that wasn't examined. Contributing factors worth flagging: no pre-release test coverage for the zero-denominator case, no alerting tied to flag changes, no automated rollback, and the alert itself fired late relative to when the issue actually began.

Now I'm drafting the action items: AI-1 fixes the division-by-zero bug with a guard and test; AI-2 adds gradual rollout with auto-rollback tied to error-rate thresholds; AI-3 speeds up alerting and pages on flag-correlated error spikes; AI-4 tightens incident record-keeping so flag changes and mitigations are logged accurately with reconciled timestamps; AI-5 has Argus's mitigation agent actually propose a flag rollback instead of stalling in a "mitigating" state without acting. For lessons learned, I'm noting the investigator identified the leading candidate fairly quickly, using the timestamp gap between early and later investigation steps as rough evidence.

I should be careful not to hardcode specific numbers in the executive summary -- better to use placeholders like {duration} and {errors_while_broken}. The symptom here was account page requests failing. Part of the "lucky" framing is that the flag was the only change made, a person noticed and manually rolled it back, and the resolution was confirmed by a person after the intent agent asked for confirmation -- despite some disconnect-related noise in the signal. Now I'll write this up.

action_items.item: Fix the zero-divisor case at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 with a guard and handling for an empty or zero denominator. Add a regression test for it, and run the account page with the flag on in pre-production.
Roll out monthly-spend-feature and other flags in stages, with an automatic halt and rollback when the account page error rate rises above its baseline during the rollout.
Alert on error-rate rise sooner, and annotate pages with flag changes made shortly before the onset so responders see the likely cause at once.
Let the Mitigation Agent propose, or perform with approval, a flag rollback when the leading candidate is a flag toggle. Record any manual rollback in the incident as an action with a verdict.

Reconcile flag change event timestamps with flag evaluation logs, to find out why the logged change falls after the onset. Make sure every flag state change, including gradual ramps, is emitted as a change event.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw account page requests fail. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to an average of {errors_while_broken} and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, so {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The failing requests raised a ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 on the account page path. These errors began in the same minute as the onset.

That code path runs only when monthly-spend-feature is on. Before the onset the flag evaluated as off for every request. In the minute the errors began, part of the evaluations were already on, and later evaluations were on.

The flag was switched on by an admin through a production flag toggle. This was the only production change read, and the flag provider's history shows a single recent flag change. Turning it on exposed live traffic to the faulty division. The record does not show why the divisor can be zero, so the chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The code at spend_summary.py:47 has no guard against a zero divisor and no test covering that case, so the flag-gated path shipped with a latent crash.
The flag moved live traffic onto the new path with no automatic check on error rate and no automatic rollback, so failures continued until a person intervened.
Detection was slow: the alert was raised {alert_raised - began} after the onset, so shoppers were failing for that gap before anyone was paged. Nothing tied the error rise to the flag change.

Argus moved to MITIGATING on the flag candidate but took no action, and the candidate was never tried. The rollback was done by hand and recorded only as a thread message, so the response record cannot show what ended the incident.

The flag change event is stamped at {P1.1}, after the onset at {began}, while flag evaluation logs show the flag on from the onset. The record cannot say when or how the flag was first enabled, so change data cannot be trusted to line up with impact.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, a share of shoppers' account page requests failed. The error rate averaged {errors_while_broken} against a normal {errors_before}, and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The cause was a feature flag, monthly-spend-feature, that was turned on. It exposed a code path on the account page that divides by zero. Argus raised the incident, found the flag as its leading cause and moved to mitigate, but took no action itself. A person rolled the flag back by hand and resolved the incident from Slack, and error rates then returned to normal.

got_lucky: The flag was the only recent production change and was easy to reverse, so a manual rollback was enough.
Latency, CPU and memory stayed flat, so the failures stayed confined to the one code path and did not spread.
went_well: The Investigator found the single production change and the matching ZeroDivisionError log line, and named the flag as the leading candidate within {T12.1 - T1.1} of the alert.
A person acted quickly with a flag rollback and confirmed it, and Argus asked for confirmation before the incident was closed as resolved.
went_wrong: Errors began at {began} but the alert came only at {alert_raised}.
Argus reached MITIGATING and took no action, so the fix depended on a person acting outside the incident's recorded actions.
The flag change time in the change record does not agree with when the flag was seen on in the logs.

input.root_cause: Account page requests hit a ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 once the monthly-spend-feature flag was evaluated as on. The new code path divides by a value that can be zero, and it reached live traffic with no guard against that and no automatic rollback.
